newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Countries prepare for sweeping Infotech trade pact.
newsitem.headline: Countries prepare for sweeping Infotech trade pact.

text.p: Negotiators gather in Geneva on Wednesday to finalise a sweeping $500 billion deal to scrap tariffs in the booming information technology trade by the year 2000 in a boost to makers of computer and telecommunication equipment.

Trade officials said 41 countries representing 92 percent of the IT market had committed themselves to the global accord, which analysts say will open the way for a vast expansion of the industry and cut costs for consumers and businesses.
The long-awaited accord has been hailed as a landmark deal which would open the way for ambitious future global pacts along with one concluded in February to liberalise trade in telecoms.

U.S., German, Japanese, South Korean and other big producers of computer and telecommunication products stand to profit from an abolition of tariffs, saving tens of millions of dollars and boosting overseas earnings, trade officials said.
Some trade diplomats cautioned that many technical questions had yet to be resolved in Geneva on the terms for countries wishing to join in, but they said a deal was essentially done.
"We've been working since midnight last night to finalise the details. We wouldn't want to jeopardise a deal we already have," said a senior diplomat from a major world trade power.
The accord was shaped in December during a Singapore ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation (WTO), which says it is confident that the participants will conclude it.
Panama recently joined the deal after Malaysia and Thailand last month, and the Czech Republic and Slovakia have promised to finalise their offers this week.

The pact cuts tariffs in four stages between 1997 and 2000 in five main product categories: computers, telecom products, semiconductors, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, software including diskettes and CD ROMs and scientific instruments.
The deal was originally championed by the United States.

But after intensive negotiations among the top trading powers in the second half of last year, the European Union agreed to come on board in Singapore and other key developed and developing countries followed suit.
Foreign ministers of the 15-member EU formally approved the accord in Brussels on Monday and asked the European Commission to make minor changes to their text and to submit it to the WTO.
Senior trade diplomats in Geneva said a "critical mass" had been reached for the implementation of the accord, under which the first tariff cuts must take place in July.
Some developing countries will be allowed to delay cuts for some products until after the year 2000.
The United States, EU and Japan are known to be unhappy with offers from key Asian states including Malaysia, Thailand and also India to maintain tariffs on some products until 2005 or 2007.
Diplomats said Washington was pushing Malaysia and Thailand to agree to tariff abolitions by 2005.

With Panama's adherence to the IT deal, confirmed participants are Australia, Canada, Costa Rica, Estonia, the 15 members of the EU, Hong Kong, Iceland, India, Indonesia, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Macau, Malaysia, New Zealand, Norway, Poland, Romania, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, Turkey and the United States.
U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, who has argued the deal will give a kick to the global economy, said earlier this month coverage was now enough for an accord.
Although the pact was negotiated outside the WTO framework, it will be incorporated into its rules and signatories will be obliged to extend its terms to all its other members.
